Project links

  • Live demo: https://cellasagfas.vercel.app/

  • CKBuilder review: CellGuard: browser-based CKB transaction policy inspector and read-only Testnet auditor · Issue #48 · Nervos-Community-Catalyst/CKBuilder-projects · GitHub

  • Completed real Testnet audit: CellGuard manually triggered chain audit · tydeptrai21042004/CellGuard@8968030 · GitHub

  • Proposed application integration: GitHub - alesfer001/CrowdCell · GitHub

1. Project Overview

CellGuard is an open-source CKB transaction policy inspector that checks application-specific transaction invariants before signing or broadcasting.

It already supports browser-based inspection, a Node.js CLI, GitHub Actions, and read-only CKB RPC verification.

CellGuard has also successfully completed a real CKB Testnet historical transaction audit, resolving actual transaction inputs and verifying the resulting capacity accounting against a configured policy.

For this Spark phase, I propose taking the next step: integrating CellGuard into a real CrowdCell transaction workflow, initially focusing on pledge transactions.

CrowdCell provides a useful test case because a pledge involves several related Cells and application-specific accounting rules that should remain consistent.

The central question is:

Can a lightweight pre-submission policy check detect unintended changes to a real CKB application’s Cell transitions, while remaining easy to integrate into its existing CCC transaction builder?

This proposal is not intended to fund another general-purpose security framework. It is a focused experiment using an existing application and a policy checker that has already been tested against real CKB chain data.

2. Applicant Background

I am the primary developer of CellGuard and have been developing open-source CKB projects through the CKBuilder program.

My previous work includes transaction lifecycle tools, Cell-based service applications, and policy verification experiments.

CellGuard has received initial CKBuilder feedback, and @Xcodes-chain has been assigned as a mentor for the project.

During the CKBuilders discussion, CrowdCell developer @alesfer001 suggested using CrowdCell pledge transactions as a practical test case for CellGuard.

The suggested checks concern the campaign Cell transition, pledge Cell, receipt Cell, and the consistency of their accounting values.

That feedback motivated this integra@alesfer001ion proposal.

3. Existing Implementation and Testnet Evidence

CellGuard is already a functioning prototype, not a proposal to build the initial inspection engine.

Implemented functionality

  • Browser-based transaction inspection and policy editing.

  • Node.js CLI with machine-readable reports and CI exit codes.

  • Exact lock/type script matching and transaction structure validation.

  • Role-based capacity accounting and recipient restrictions.

  • Optional typed-Cell capacity preservation.

  • Required dependency and since checks.

  • Read-only CKB RPC verification and historical transaction lookup.

  • Synthetic CrowdCell policy regression tests.

  • A preliminary CrowdCell transaction preflight bridge.

Completed real CKB Testnet validation

CellGuard has already been exercised against an actual committed CKB Testnet transaction through its GitHub Actions audit workflow.

Evidence:

github.com

Add RPC-validated public CKB Testnet consolidation policy

CellGuard manually triggered chain audit #2

The successful historical audit reported:

Measurement Result
Audit result MATCH

The public transaction hash used in the audit setup was:

0x6fb7350b37463df3e31fcfd5558651193fb8ff5dd3c824e0b1afe31892b90448

The audit demonstrates that CellGuard can resolve historical CKB inputs and evaluate real transaction capacity accounting using RPC-backed evidence.

Its limitations are important: this particular transaction was a consolidation transaction, not a CrowdCell pledge. It does not demonstrate a live CrowdCell contract exploit, an independent CKB consensus proof, or a completed CrowdCell pre-signing integration.

The existing synthetic CrowdCell tests are separate from this real-chain evidence.

These capabilities and previous Testnet experiments are already completed and are not being requested for retroactive funding.

4. Problem and Motivation

CKB applications construct transactions that consume existing Cells and create new Cells.

For stateful applications, a transaction may involve multiple related outputs whose capacities, scripts, and data must satisfy application-specific conditions.

For example, a CrowdCell pledge may involve:

  • consuming and recreating the campaign Cell;

  • recording the increase in pledged value;

  • creating a pledge Cell;

  • issuing a corresponding receipt Cell;

  • preserving required script identities and accounting relationships.

An application developer may want an additional safeguard before submission to detect a malformed transaction, such as an unexpected output recipient or an inconsistent pledge/receipt amount.

CKB scripts enforce their programmed consensus conditions, and CCC handles transaction construction and signing. CellGuard does not replace either.

Instead, CellGuard evaluates a separately defined application policy against the transaction that the application intends to submit.

The question is whether this additional check provides practical value without creating unnecessary complexity.

The CrowdCell pilot is intended to answer that question using a real application rather than synthetic examples alone.

5. Proposed Solution

The proposed experiment will connect CellGuard to one current CrowdCell transaction path: pledge creation.

Step 1 — Establish a reviewed policy

Identify the relevant current CrowdCell contract deployment, exact script identities, transaction fields, and permitted capacity changes.

The policy will be based on actual contract semantics and transaction-builder behavior, not on assumptions derived from illustrative examples.

Step 2 — Integrate policy verification

CrowdCell constructs the transaction through its existing CCC workflow.

CellGuard inspects the transaction before it proceeds to submission.

The intended integration has two stages:

  1. Local policy check: Detect unintended outputs, incorrect script identities, and accounting inconsistencies before requesting a signature where possible.

  2. Optional signed-transaction preflight: Inspect the exact signed transaction using read-only CKB RPC before broadcast.

A failed or inconclusive required check blocks progression in the pilot.

Step 3 — Validate against real and mutated transactions

The pilot will use a legitimate CrowdCell Testnet transaction as a positive example.

Controlled mutations of its transaction structure will be used to verify whether CellGuard detects unintended capacity transfers, incorrect scripts, or inconsistent accounting.

Invalid fixtures will be checked locally and will not be broadcast to the public network.

6. Technical Architecture

Technology

  • JavaScript ES modules / Node.js 22

  • CellGuard policy engine and CLI

  • CrowdCell’s existing CCC-based transaction builder

  • CKB Testnet JSON-RPC

  • GitHub Actions

Proposed workflow

flowchart TD
    A["CrowdCell constructs transaction with CCC"] --> B["CellGuard local policy inspection"]
    B --> C{"Policy result"}
    C -->|FAIL or INCONCLUSIVE| D["Stop and report findings"]
    C -->|PASS| E["Sign with existing wallet"]
    E --> F["Optional read-only signed TX preflight"]
    F --> G{"Required checks pass?"}
    G -->|No| D
    G -->|Yes| H["Submit unchanged signed transaction"]

CellGuard will not require a new database, background service, custody system, or CKB smart contract.

The pilot will use a versioned policy tied to a particular CrowdCell deployment. It will not assume that the same policy remains valid after contract upgrades.

7. New Work Requested from Spark

The proposed grant supports application integration and validation, rather than development of CellGuard’s existing policy engine.

The new work is limited to:

  1. Establishing a real CrowdCell pledge policy for the current deployment.

  2. Connecting the policy to the actual CCC transaction-building path.

  3. Demonstrating positive and negative policy decisions using current application transaction data.

  4. Publishing a reproducible evidence package linked to the deployment and policy version.

  5. Obtaining feedback on whether the integration is useful and sufficiently lightweight.

The existing real CKB Testnet historical audit will be included as baseline evidence, not represented as a new funded milestone.

8. Milestones and Timeline

Milestone Timeline Acceptance criteria
M1 — Deployment-specific policy Week 1 A documented policy for the current CrowdCell pledge transition, with exact script identities
M2 — Transaction-builder integration Week 2 Local policy checks and optional signed RPC preflight wired to the selected transaction path
M3 — Real application validation Week 3 A legitimate CrowdCell Testnet transaction is checked, and controlled negative variants are rejected
M4 — Independent evaluation Week 4 Reproducibility instructions, CI tests, demo, and a report of developer feedback

M1 — Policy specification

Review the deployed CrowdCell transaction format and the relevant source code.

Document which Cell transitions and values must be preserved, and which changes are legitimate.

Request confirmation of application-specific assumptions from the CrowdCell developer where possible.

M2 — Integration

Adapt CellGuard’s existing CrowdCell bridge to the selected pledge builder.

The integration must preserve the original application’s signing and submission behavior, with CellGuard operating as an optional verification step.

Provide fixtures and tests for normal and intentionally malformed transactions.

M3 — Testnet validation

Use a genuine transaction associated with the selected current CrowdCell deployment.

Publish the transaction hash, policy version, source revision, relevant Cell evidence, and read-only inspection result.

Show that the valid transaction passes, while modified variants fail or remain inconclusive as appropriate.

This is distinct from the historical Testnet consolidation audit already completed.

M4 — Developer feedback and closure

Publish a short demo and reproduction guide.

Invite the CrowdCell developer and other CKBuilders to test or review the integration.

Document whether the policy is useful, whether it introduces false positives, and how much additional work is required to adopt it.

The final report will distinguish completed tests, independently reviewed results, and any remaining limitations.

9. Funding Breakdown

Total requested: $500 USD equivalent in CKB.

Work Budget
Current CrowdCell deployment analysis and reviewed policy $100
CCC transaction-builder integration and negative tests $200
CrowdCell-specific Testnet validation and reproducible evidence $125
Documentation, demo, developer feedback and reporting $75
Total $500

The amount is a modest contribution to the four-week experiment, not reimbursement for previously completed CellGuard development.

Existing Testnet historical-audit functionality, browser inspection, CLI implementation, synthetic regressions and the preliminary integration bridge are excluded from the funded scope.

No recurring database or paid backend infrastructure is proposed.

Actual use of funds will be summarized at completion.

10. Deliverables and How to Verify

Deliverable Verification method
Current deployment policy Inspect the documented script identities and application-specific invariants
CrowdCell pledge integration Execute the integration with representative CCC transaction data
Positive transaction evidence Verify a real CrowdCell Testnet transaction hash and policy result
Negative regression tests Run local tests showing malformed variants are rejected
Fail-closed behavior Confirm that missing required evidence never produces PASS
Reproducibility Run the tests from a clean checkout using the documented commands
Developer feedback Inspect the review and usability report

Existing verification commands

git clone https://github.com/tydeptrai21042004/CellGuard.git
cd CellGuard

npm run check
npm run test:policies
npm run test:crowdcell-integration

The existing repository provides these commands for the current test suite and integration bridge.

The funded release will provide a dedicated reproduction procedure for the selected live CrowdCell deployment.

Required positive and negative cases

Positive case: The selected legitimate CrowdCell pledge satisfies the reviewed policy.

Negative case A: An unauthorized capacity change is detected.

Negative case B: Incorrect campaign, pledge, or receipt script identities are rejected.

Negative case C: An accounting inconsistency is detected according to the actual contract’s rules.

Inconclusive case: A required input Cell, dependency, or RPC observation is unavailable, so the tool does not report a successful verification.

The final evidence will include the exact source revision, transaction hash, policy definition, result, and reproduction commands.

CellGuard remains an application-policy checker, not a formal contract-security proof or independent guarantee of consensus validity.

11. CKB Ecosystem Value

The pilot is grounded in CKB’s Cell model rather than a generic blockchain transaction format.

It focuses on application-level correctness conditions involving:

  • exact lock and type script identities;

  • Cell capacity changes;

  • typed Cell preservation;

  • transaction dependencies;

  • application-specific accounting and recipient rules.

The integration complements existing infrastructure.

CCC remains responsible for transaction construction and signing. CKB scripts remain responsible for on-chain enforcement. CKB RPC provides node observations.

CellGuard provides a separate, optional policy check against the application’s intended transaction behavior.

Unlike a broad security framework, this experiment has one target application, one selected transaction path, and directly testable outcomes.

The practical value will be evaluated by whether the pilot catches meaningful mistakes at a sufficiently low integration cost.

12. Risks and Scope Control

Risk Mitigation
Policy assumptions do not match CrowdCell contracts Pin the current deployment and request maintainer review
New CrowdCell deployment changes script identities Version the policy and reject mismatched identities
Policy incorrectly rejects legitimate transactions Test against representative valid transactions and document false positives
Maintainer cannot participate Publish the independent pilot and disclose the lack of official integration
Testnet RPC data is incomplete Report INCONCLUSIVE instead of silently passing
Scope exceeds four weeks Limit work to pledge creation; defer finalize, refund and release

The project will not include new on-chain contracts, Mainnet deployment, general-purpose auditing certification, or modifications to CrowdCell’s consensus rules.

13. Open Source and Reporting

CellGuard is published under the MIT license.

All new policy definitions, integration code, tests, and evidence documentation will be made publicly available.

I will provide weekly updates in the Spark thread, covering completed work, commits, validation results, and problems encountered.

The completion report will include:

  • Planned versus completed milestones.

  • Real Testnet evidence and reproducible policy tests.

  • Independent developer feedback where available.

  • Known limitations and incorrect-policy risks.

  • Funding usage and lessons learned.

Final Objective

CellGuard has already demonstrated successful policy auditing against real CKB Testnet transaction data. This Spark experiment will determine whether that existing capability can become a useful, lightweight policy safeguard inside an actual CrowdCell transaction workflow.

The intended result is a verifiable application integration, not another general-purpose infrastructure layer.

Thank you for considering the proposal. I welcome feedback on the selected transaction path, deployment-specific policy assumptions, and the proposed verification method.

posts.name: Ayoub Lesfer
posts.cooked: Hey Dang, nice to see this, and happy to review the pledge profile once you’ve pinned it. A few things that should save you time. The live deployment is the one in deployment/deployed-contracts-testnet.json (redeployed Oct 31), that’s what crowdcell.vercel.app runs. The fallback hashes in off-chain/indexer/src/index.ts are still the old ones, I’ll fix that, so don’t take them from there. Also the pledge tx the app sends isn’t TransactionBuilder.createPledge, it’s built in off-chain/frontend/src/app/campaigns/[id]/page.tsx: the campaign cell goes in, then campaign + pledge + receipt come out, with the campaign capacity and scripts unchanged and total pledged bumped by the pledge amount. The natural hook is right after completeFeeBy and before signer.sendTransaction. One thing to plan for: when two pledges race for the campaign cell, the page rebuilds the tx on top of the new one and asks again, up to 3 times, so the check has to run on every attempt, not once. And Tung is working on an opt-in session version of that same retry path, so worth syncing with him so you don’t both hook the same spot in different ways.

posts.name: Dang Ba Ty
posts.cooked:
Thanks @Ayoub_Lesfer, this is really helpful!

I’ll use deployment/deployed-contracts-testnet.json as the source for the current script identities and inspect the pledge flow in off-chain/frontend/src/app/campaigns/[id]/page.tsx, rather than relying on TransactionBuilder.createPledge or the outdated indexer fallbacks.

I’ll place the CellGuard check after completeFeeBy and before signer.sendTransaction, ensuring it runs again whenever the transaction is rebuilt during a retry. The initial policy will focus on preserving the campaign cell’s capacity and scripts, verifying the pledged amount update, and checking the corresponding pledge and receipt outputs.

I’ll also coordinate with Tung to avoid conflicting changes to the retry path.

Once the deployment-specific policy and integration are ready, I’ll share the implementation and test results here for review. Thanks again for pointing me to the correct transaction flow!

posts.name: 行天春彦
posts.cooked:
Hello, @Dangbaty2004，

Thank you for taking the time to prepare and submit this proposal, and for providing detailed documentation. The committee has completed its review and, unfortunately, has decided not to approve the CellGuard × CrowdCell proposal at this time.

We want to be candid about the reasons for this decision:

The project scope falls outside the Spark Program’s support remit: The proposal’s core is to add an intermediary layer for security audits to an existing project (CrowdCell). We believe that this type of effort—building a policy-checking layer on top of another application’s transaction flow—falls outside Spark’s funding scope.

We truly appreciate all the effort your team has put in. Please keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!

Best regards
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

posts.name: Dang Ba Ty
posts.cooked:
Hello @xingtianchunyan and the Spark Program Committee,

Thank you for reviewing the CellGuard × CrowdCell proposal and clarifying the program’s scope.

I understand the decision and will continue the CellGuard integration work independently through the CKBuilder process.

For a potential future Spark application, I am considering a more product-oriented direction: SkillPass Care, a CKB-based transferable warranty application for second-hand products.

The underlying SkillPass protocol has already demonstrated issuance, ownership transfer, and authorization on CKB Testnet. A new proposal would focus exclusively on work that has not yet been completed: integrating real Testnet ownership into the warranty application, validating the complete transfer-and-service lifecycle, and conducting an initial user/provider pilot.

Before preparing a full application, I would appreciate your guidance on whether this type of early-stage product validation is more aligned with Spark’s funding scope.

Thank you again for your time and feedback.

posts.cooked: @Dangbaty2004 sorry it didn’t go through on Spark, still keen to have CellGuard hooked into the pledge flow, ping me when there’s a PR and I’ll go through it
